problem: It says the whole double-frequency component is the exchange with stored energy. That is false: p(t)=P(1−cos2ωt)−Q sin2ωt. The cos2ωt part is pulsation of real power and exists even in a pure resistor, where no energy is stored. A student will misunderstand why p(t) goes negative.
fix: Say: The double-frequency component has zero average and does not add to P. Its quadrature part (the Q sin2ωt part) represents exchange with stored energy; its in-phase part is the twice-frequency pulsation of real power. In a pure resistor, the oscillation is real-power pulsation, not stored energy.

problem: It calls reactive power 'the energy traded'. Q is power (rate of energy exchange), not energy; the unit is VAR, not joule. This can make students confuse reactive power with reactive energy.
fix: Say 'it is the rate at which energy is exchanged with inductance or capacitance' or 'it represents reactive energy traded back and forth'.

problem: The exception 'unless their power factors are equal' is incomplete. Two 100 VA loads at 0.8 lagging and 0.8 leading have equal power-factor magnitude but total |S|=160 VA, not 200 VA, because their Q values cancel.
fix: Say 'unless their power factors are equal and of the same sign (both lagging or both leading)'.
